summary.text: The block [2,4,2,4,2[0m has cumulative offsets [0,2,6,8,12,14[0m, which cover every residue class modulo 5[0m. Thus in any occurrence one of the six corresponding primes is divisible by 5[0m and hence equals 5[0m, forcing the initial prime to be at most 5[0m and leaving only finitely many possible starting indices.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
p_1=2<p_2=3<p_3=5<p_4=7<\cdots
\]
denote the primes in increasing order, and let
\[
a(r)=p_{r+1}-p_r\qquad(r\ge 1)
\]
be the sequence of gaps between consecutive primes.

We disprove the assertion by taking the particular values
\[
n=3,\qquad m=4.
\]
Thus the relevant block has length \(m+1=5\).

The primes through \(19\) are
\[
2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(3)&=p_4-p_3=7-5=2,\\
a(4)&=p_5-p_4=11-7=4,\\
a(5)&=p_6-p_5=13-11=2,\\
a(6)&=p_7-p_6=17-13=4,\\
a(7)&=p_8-p_7=19-17=2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore the finite subsequence beginning at \(n=3\) is
\[
(a(3),a(4),a(5),a(6),a(7))=(2,4,2,4,2).
\]
This is indeed a legitimate instance covered by the conjecture, since \(3>2\) and \(4\ge 0\).

We now show that this block cannot occur infinitely often. Suppose it occurs beginning at some positive index \(k\). Put
\[
q=p_k.
\]
Since the five successive gaps beginning at \(p_k\) are assumed to be \(2,4,2,4,2\), adding the gaps cumulatively gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
p_k&=q,\\
p_{k+1}&=q+2,\\
p_{k+2}&=q+2+4=q+6,\\
p_{k+3}&=q+2+4+2=q+8,\\
p_{k+4}&=q+2+4+2+4=q+12,\\
p_{k+5}&=q+2+4+2+4+2=q+14.
\end{aligned}
\]
In particular, all six numbers
\[
q,\ q+2,\ q+6,\ q+8,\ q+12,\ q+14
\]
are prime. (They are in fact consecutive primes, although only their primality is needed for the modular obstruction.)

Consider these six offsets modulo \(5\). Their residues are
\[
0,2,6,8,12,14\equiv 0,2,1,3,2,4\pmod 5.
\]
Thus the offsets include every residue class modulo \(5\). It follows that, whatever the residue of \(q\) modulo \(5\), at least one of the six displayed primes is divisible by \(5\). Explicitly, the cases are as follows:

* If \(q\equiv 0\pmod 5\), then \(5\mid q\).
* If \(q\equiv 1\pmod 5\), then \(q+14\equiv 0\pmod 5\).
* If \(q\equiv 2\pmod 5\), then \(q+8\equiv 0\pmod 5\).
* If \(q\equiv 3\pmod 5\), then \(q+2\equiv 0\pmod 5\).
* If \(q\equiv 4\pmod 5\), then \(q+6\equiv 0\pmod 5\).

In every case, one of
\[
q,\ q+2,\ q+6,\ q+8,\ q+14
\]
(and hence one of the six primes in the run) is divisible by \(5\). A prime divisible by \(5\) must equal \(5\). Since every one of these numbers is at least \(q\), we conclude that
\[
q\le 5.
\]
But \(q=p_k\), and the fourth prime is \(p_4=7>5\). Since the primes are strictly increasing, \(p_k\le 5\) implies
\[
k\le 3.
\]
Therefore every positive starting index at which the block \((2,4,2,4,2)\) occurs belongs to the finite set \(\{1,2,3\}\). If one extends the indexing to include an artificial zeroth term \(a(0)=0\), then \(k=0\) cannot realize this block because its first entry would be \(0\); in any event all possible starting indices lie in the finite set \(\{0,1,2,3\}\).

For completeness, among the positive indices at most \(3\), the block actually occurs only at \(k=3\): at \(k=1\) its first term would be \(a(1)=3-2=1\), while at \(k=2\) its first two terms are
\[
(a(2),a(3))=(5-3,7-5)=(2,2),
\]
not \((2,4)\). At \(k=3\), the calculation above shows that the entire block is \((2,4,2,4,2)\).

Hence the occurrence set of the finite subsequence
\[
a(3),a(4),a(5),a(6),a(7)
\]
is finite (indeed, it has exactly one positive starting index), rather than infinite. This single choice \(n=3\), \(m=4\) contradicts the universal conjecture.

The underlying obstruction is precisely that the prime constellation with cumulative offsets
\[
\{0,2,6,8,12,14\}
\]
is not admissible: modulo \(5\), those offsets cover every residue class. It can occur only when the forced multiple of \(5\) is the exceptional prime \(5\) itself, and therefore it cannot recur arbitrarily far out among the primes. Thus the appeal to the prime \(k\)-tuple conjecture does not apply to this block.
